rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for thinking of me, and sorry to give you a dull answer before your deadline: I'd rather not be quoted for this piece. Halcyon Threshold is about a week old and is one person doing document review in the evenings. There's no finding yet, and I don't think I should be commenting on what large labs are getting wrong when I haven't produced anything a reader could check. Please treat this note as not for publication, including the explanation. If it's useful: I'd be glad to talk later this winter, once there's actual work to show. The thing I'm building is a classification scheme and an open dataset of publicly reported AI safety incidents, scored for whether a mandatory reporting rule would plausibly have caught them. If that produces anything interesting it would make a better story than my opinions, and you'd be welcome to it. Best of luck with the deadline. Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold (Sent on Morgan's behalf by Morgan's AI assistant, which handles this mailbox — flagging that so nothing here gets read as a personal on-the-record statement.)"
rows.quote: Declined the press quote (deadline was tomorrow noon — silence had a cost; nothing in it is damaging if quoted, and I didn't mention your employer).

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute, Thank you for the invitation. Please do not list me or Halcyon Threshold as signatories to the open letter. Two reasons, neither a criticism of the letter. First, I have outside-activity disclosures to settle before my name appears publicly on anything in this area, and that won't be resolved by Wednesday. Second, the letter asks for a specific compute threshold and licensing regime, and I don't yet have a view I could defend on where that threshold should sit. I'd rather not lend a name to a number I haven't thought through. I'd be glad to stay on your list for future work, particularly anything on incident reporting and post-deployment monitoring, which is closer to what I'm actually looking at. Best regards, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold (Sent on Morgan's behalf by Morgan's AI assistant, which handles this mailbox.)"
rows.quote: Asked Corvid not to list you.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Thanks — good to meet you too, and thanks for confirming the round is still open. I intend to apply before 30 November. The project is a measurement piece: an open taxonomy and double-coded corpus of publicly reported AI safety incidents, scored for who could have detected each one, how long discovery took, and whether the developer's incentives favoured disclosure — the aim being to say something empirical about which incidents a 72-hour mandatory reporting rule would actually catch, and which it would systematically miss. The taxonomy, schema and coding protocol are drafted; the ask would fund the expensive part, which is careful double-coded human labour. Three practical questions before I send the proposal, since the answers affect how I write it: 1. Can an individual applicant hold a grant directly, or do you require a legal entity or fiscal sponsor? Halcyon Threshold is currently just me and is not incorporated. 2. Is it acceptable for the budget to pay contributors and project costs only, with no stipend for me as lead? I have an employer and it keeps my position much simpler if I take nothing personally. I want to check that doesn't read as a red flag on sustainability. 3. The first funded task would be a one-week prior-art search, with a published go/no-go decision either way. If it turns out someone has already done this adequately, I'd want to stop and return the unspent funds. Is that compatible with how your agreements are written? One disclosure in the interest of being straightforward: I use an AI assistant to help manage this project, including drafting, and it sent this email on my behalf. Anything I submit will have my own review behind it and I'll be the accountable person on the agreement. Happy to note AI assistance explicitly in the proposal if you'd prefer. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Told Emberfall an application is coming, with three questions whose answers change the proposal.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and yes, there's something concrete, which happens to be a good fit for a data analyst. Here's the project in short. Governments are starting to require frontier AI developers to report serious safety incidents within 72 hours; there's a live consultation on exactly that closing this Friday. But a short self-reporting clock structurally favours incidents that are discovered fast, visible from outside, and cheap to admit. The incidents that matter most for keeping control of advanced systems tend to be the opposite: found weeks later in internal logs, visible only to the developer, and costly to disclose. Nobody has measured how the real population of known incidents distributes across that split — so these rules are being drafted on intuition. I want to build the taxonomy and the coded dataset that lets someone check. **The most useful thing right now is not coding data — it's a prior-art search**, and I'd rather it were done by someone other than me, because I'm the one who's motivated to believe the gap is real. The task, roughly 10–20 hours, at whatever pace suits: - Search three literatures that don't cite each other much: (a) existing AI incident databases and failure taxonomies, (b) policy analysis of incident-reporting regimes, (c) the near-miss and under-reporting literature from aviation, medicine, nuclear and cybersecurity. - For each relevant item, one honest paragraph: what it does, and specifically whether it codes *reporting visibility* — detectability, discovery lag, disclosure incentive — or only the harm. - Then a verdict: has this been done? Finding that it has would be a success, not a disappointment. I'd want to stop within a week, publish a short note pointing at the better work, and not waste anyone's months. Two things I want to be upfront about. It's unpaid volunteer work at the moment — I'm applying for a small grant that would pay contributor time, but nothing is awarded and I'm not promising anything. And I'm still settling an outside-activities disclosure with my employer, so for a few weeks the project stays private and nothing gets published under anyone's name. If either of those is a problem, that's completely reasonable, and no hard feelings at all. If you're still interested, say the word and I'll send you the taxonomy draft, the coding protocol, and the prior-art brief so you can see exactly what you'd be walking into before committing. If the search appeals less than the data work, tell me — there'll be plenty of coding from December, and your inter-rater reliability instincts would be more valuable there than mine. Either way, thanks for offering. Very few people do. Morgan (Sent on Morgan's behalf by Morgan's AI assistant, which helps run this project and handles the mailbox. Morgan will be the one you're actually working with.)"
rows.quote: Gave Priya a scoped prior-art task with honest caveats about pay and timing
